Fellow
FEL-oh
n.
From Old Norse felagi, one who lays down money with another, a partner. Webster 1828: a companion; an associate; one of the same kind; and, in contempt, a mean or worthless man. The Authorized Version uses every one of those senses, including the contemptuous one — and once, astonishingly, of the Messiah beside the LORD of hosts.

Biblical Definition

Fellow in the KJV usually means the other man. Moses asks the aggressor, Wherefore smitest thou thy fellow? (Exodus 2:13). In Gideon’s camp one Midianite tells a dream and his fellow answered (Judges 7:14). In Saul’s rout every man's sword was against his fellow (1 Samuel 14:20). Jonah’s sailors speak every one to his fellow (Jonah 1:7). Ecclesiastes turns it into the argument for companionship: if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up (Ecclesiastes 4:10). The contemptuous sense is also biblical — Achish sneers, shall this fellow come into my house? (1 Samuel 21:15), and Jehu is called this mad fellow (2 Kings 9:11). But the weightiest use is Zechariah’s: Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man that is my fellow, saith the LORD of hosts: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered (Zechariah 13:7). The Hebrew word there means one joined as an equal, and the LORD of hosts uses it of the shepherd He will smite — a verse our Lord quoted of Himself on the night He was betrayed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives FELLOW as a companion; an associate; one of the same kind; an equal; and, in a lower sense, a mean or worthless man used in contempt. The KJV employs the full range.

expand to see more

FELLOW, n. — A companion; an associate.

One of the same kind; as, the horse and his fellow.

An equal; one of the same rank or station.

A person of low condition; used in contempt; as, a mean fellow.

Webster’s third sense — an equal — is the one that makes Zechariah 13:7 so heavy. The LORD of hosts names the smitten shepherd as the man who is His fellow, which is a claim of equality no mere prophet could bear.

Key Scripture

Exodus 2:13 — "And when he went out the second day, behold, two men of the Hebrews strove together: and he said to him that did the wrong, Wherefore smitest thou thy fellow?"

1 Samuel 14:20 — "And Saul and all the people that were with him assembled themselves, and they came to the battle: and, behold, every man's sword was against his fellow, and there was a very great discomfiture."

Ecclesiastes 4:10 — "For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up."

Zechariah 13:7 — "Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man that is my fellow, saith the LORD of hosts: smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered: and I will turn mine hand upon the little ones."

Hebrews 1:9 — "Thou hast loved righteousness, and hated iniquity; therefore God, even thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss is a forgotten proof-text: Zechariah 13:7 is one of the strongest Old Testament witnesses to the deity of the Messiah, and it is now rarely preached as such.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The English word has drifted toward informality, but nothing is being contested. What has been lost is the doctrinal force of Zechariah 13:7. The LORD of hosts calls the shepherd the man that is my fellow — the Hebrew noun denotes an associate of the same standing, and it is used elsewhere in Leviticus of a man’s neighbour and equal. God does not call prophets or kings His fellow. That He does so of the smitten shepherd, and that our Lord applied the verse to Himself the night He was taken (Matthew 26:31), makes it a witness both to His deity and to the deliberateness of the cross: the sword is commanded to awake, and the commanding voice is the Father’s.

The principle to recover alongside it is Ecclesiastes 4:10, which the age needs and resists. Woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up is a plain argument against the isolated Christian life. The New Testament turns it into church membership — not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, bearing one another’s burdens, confessing faults one to another. A believer who has arranged his life so that no fellow is close enough to lift him has arranged it against the wisdom of this verse, and Hebrews 1:9 shows the pattern is not beneath the dignity of the Son, who is anointed above His fellows but is not without them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Several words lie behind the English. Rea' is a neighbour or companion; 'amith in Zechariah 13:7 is an associate of equal standing; the Greek metochos in Hebrews 1:9 means a partner or partaker.

expand to see more

Hebrew rea' (H7453) — friend, neighbour, companion; wherefore smitest thou thy fellow? (Exodus 2:13), and the word in love thy neighbour.

Hebrew 'amith (H5997) — an associate, one of equal standing; the man that is my fellow (Zechariah 13:7), used elsewhere only in Leviticus.

Hebrew chaber (H2270) — a companion, one joined; behind the one will lift up his fellow (Ecclesiastes 4:10).

Greek metochos (G3353) — a partner, partaker; above thy fellows (Hebrews 1:9), and the word for those made partakers of Christ (Hebrews 3:14).

Greek hetairos (G2083) — comrade; our Lord’s address to Judas in Gethsemane, Friend, wherefore art thou come?

Usage

"Every man's sword was against his fellow (1 Samuel 14:20) — the confusion God sends on an enemy army."

"Woe to him that is alone when he falleth (Ecclesiastes 4:10) — the case against the isolated life."

"The man that is my fellow, saith the LORD of hosts (Zechariah 13:7) — an associate of equal standing with God, quoted by Christ of Himself."
